hints.title: Work with the squared roots
hints.body: The given polynomial contains only even powers. Set u=x2 so its quadratic roots represent the two cosine squares.
hints.recap: The signs of the original cosine roots disappear when using their squares.
hints.pitfall: A root of the quadratic in the squared variable is not yet a root of the quartic.
hints.pause: Write the quadratic satisfied by the two cosine squares.

recall.reminder: A polynomial in even powers may be a quadratic in the square of its variable.

hints.title: Relate the old and new squared roots
hints.body: For each angle, sin2=1−cos2. If v is the desired sine square, express the old variable u in terms of v.
hints.recap: The identity gives a simple transformation of the quadratic roots.
hints.pitfall: Apply the transformation to the squares; taking a square root too early complicates the signs.
hints.pause: Substitute the relation into the original quadratic.

hints.title: Return to a polynomial with signed roots
hints.body: Expand the transformed quadratic and collect its powers of v. Then replace v by x2, so both signs of each sine value are included.
hints.recap: Replacing a squared magnitude by the square of the polynomial variable restores the positive and negative roots.
hints.pitfall: The final requested equation is quartic, not quadratic.
hints.pause: Complete the expansion, write the quartic and check the root correspondence.

recall.reminder: A change of variable must be reversed to obtain an equation for the quantity actually requested.

solution:
If u is either cos2θ or cos2β, then 7u2−6u+1=0. The corresponding sine square is v=1−u.

Substituting u=1−v gives 7(1−v)2−6(1−v)+1=0, which simplifies to 7v2−8v+2=0. Therefore the requested roots satisfy 7x4−8x2+2=0.

For completeness, the original squared roots (3±2)/7 are distinct and lie between 0 and 1. Their complements are also distinct and positive, so the transformed quartic gives precisely the two required positive magnitudes and their negatives. Answer B.
knowledgePattern: Transform the quadratic in squared cosine using sine squared equals one minus cosine squared
